summary:
Echoes of Exploration is a free digital museum that asks a simple question: what remains when a space mission ends? We built an accessible website with 18 exhibits across three galleries (The Moon, Mars, and Beyond Mars), featuring spacecraft and instruments from the Apollo laser reflectors to Spirit, InSight, Ingenuity, Pioneer, and Kepler. Each exhibit introduces the object in its own voice through three questions: Who am I? What did I help discover? What did I leave humanity? Visitors can then read an imagined postcard from the spacecraft, clearly labelled as fiction, and open the official NASA source behind every fact.

The project turns NASA's mission archives into short, story-led experiences for students, teachers, and families, while keeping science and imagination clearly separate. It includes search and gallery filters, visit progress, optional narration, a full register of 26 NASA sources and image credits, and works on phones and with a keyboard, without collecting personal data.

Space missions end, but their discoveries keep shaping what we know. Echoes of Exploration helps young audiences see that legacy and learn to check where knowledge comes from.

Live site: https://sbnmkyl.github.io/echoes-of-exploration/
details:
What it does and how it works
Echoes of Exploration is a free, browser-based digital museum about what space missions leave behind after they end. Visitors walk through three galleries (The Moon, Mars, and Beyond Mars) and 18 exhibits, from the Apollo laser reflectors and Surveyor 3 to Spirit, InSight, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10 and Kepler. Opening an exhibit shows the spacecraft answering three questions in its own voice: Who am I? What did I help discover? What did I leave humanity? Below the facts is an imagined postcard from the spacecraft, clearly labelled as creative writing, and a link to the official NASA page behind every fact. Visitors can search and filter exhibits, track how many they have explored, and listen to optional narration. A sources page lists all 26 NASA references and the credit for every image.

Benefits and intended impact
NASA’s mission information is rich but spread across many pages and often written for specialists. We wanted young learners, teachers and families to meet these missions as stories they remember, while also learning to check where a fact comes from. A teacher can open a single exhibit as a short classroom starter. Our goal is that every visitor leaves with one question they want to explore further.

How we built it
We planned the museum structure, chose the 18 exhibits, collected the NASA sources and set the content rules ourselves. For example: no claim goes beyond what NASA states, and every piece of fiction carries a visible label. We used AI coding assistants to turn this specification into the website and to refine the presentation layout (details in the AI section). We then reviewed the content, checked it against the sources and tested the site.

Languages: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript ; exhibit and source data in JSON, with CSV registers

Browser features: Web Speech API for narration; local storage for visit progress

Hosting & version control: GitHub, GitHub Pages, GitHub Actions

Testing: automated acceptance checks , a content check script , manual tests on laptops and phones

Content sources: NASA mission pages and NASA imagery only

How creative is it?
Instead of a list of facts, each spacecraft tells its own story, and the postcards add emotion. Fact and fiction never mix, though: they look different and are always labelled. The museum format makes learning feel like a visit rather than a lesson.

What we considered

Scientific accuracy: careful wording for sensitive claims such as water on Mars or each spacecraft’s current status

Honesty: creative text is always labelled, every fact links to NASA, and the project states that it is not affiliated with NASA

Image rights: original credits and captions are kept for every image

Accessibility: keyboard navigation, readable text, mobile support; narration is optional and the text is always visible

Privacy: no sign-up and no personal data; progress stays in the visitor’s own browser

Our team

Ali Tuna-Project lead & concept: shaped the central question, coordinated the team and timeline, managed the submission

Toprak- Research: selected the exhibits and gathered mission information from NASA sources

Ahmet Selim- Fact-checking & sources: verified every fact, built the source and image-credit registers

Ömer Faruk- Creative writing: wrote and edited the imagined postcards and the spacecraft’s voice

Yavuz Selim- Design & accessibility: visual direction, gallery layout, mobile and keyboard testing

Yavuz- Development & deployment: wrote the technical specification, guided and reviewed the AI-assisted code, published the site on GitHub Pages
